picks.title: Differentiable Programming for Differential Equations: A Review
picks.abstract: The differentiable programming paradigm is a cornerstone of modern scientific computing. It refers to numerical methods for computing the gradient of a numerical model’s output. Many scientific models are based on differential equations, in which differentiable programming plays a crucial role in calculating model sensitivities, inverting model parameters, and training hybrid models that combine differential equations with data-driven approaches. Furthermore, recognizing the strong synergies between inverse methods and machine learning offers the opportunity to establish a coherent framework applicable to both fields. Differentiating functions based on the numerical solution of differential equations is nontrivial. Numerous methods based on a wide variety of paradigms have been proposed in the literature, each with pros and cons specific to the type of problem investigated. Here, we provide a comprehensive review of existing techniques to compute derivatives of numerical solutions of differential equations. We first discuss the importance of gradients of solutions of differential equations in a variety of scientific domains. Second, we lay out and compare the mathematical foundations of the various approaches. Third, we cover computational considerations and explore the solutions available in modern scientific software. Last but not least, we provide best practices and recommendations for practitioners. We hope that this work accelerates the fusion of scientific models and data and fosters a modern approach to scientific modeling.

picks.title: Higgsino dark matter interpretation of the LUX-ZEPLIN 248 keV nuclear-recoil event
picks.abstract: We propose Higgsino dark matter as a potential interpretation of the $248~\mathrm{keV}$ nuclear-recoil event of interest reported by the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment. LZ studied several rare background processes and detector effects in detail, but did not identify any as a likely explanation of the event. A nearly pure Higgsino naturally realizes inelastic dark matter through the off-diagonal $Z$ coupling of two nearly degenerate neutral Majorana states separated by a mass splitting $δ$. The same electroweak interaction fixes the inelastic Higgsino-nucleon scattering cross section, rather than leaving it as a free parameter. We show that the predicted Higgsino inelastic scattering cross section approaches the published LZ two-sided 90% confidence interval for a Higgsino mass $m_{\widetilde H}\sim1~\mathrm{TeV}$ and a mass splitting $δ\sim350~\mathrm{keV}$.

picks.title: The Gopakumar--Vafa finiteness conjecture
picks.abstract: The Gopakumar--Vafa conjecture predicts that the BPS invariants of a symplectic 6-manifold, defined in terms of the Gromov--Witten invariants, are integers and all but finitely many vanish in every homology class. The integrality part of this conjecture was proved earlier by Ionel and Parker. This article proves the finiteness part. The proof relies on a modification of Ionel and Parker's cluster formalism using results from geometric measure theory.

picks.title: (LRDs) 2 : The Low-ReDshift Little Red Dots Survey. II. DESI DR1 Sample
picks.abstract: JWST has revealed a substantial population of “Little Red Dots” (LRDs) at z > 4, challenging conventional active galactic muclei (AGN) frameworks. However, the low-redshift regime remains largely unexplored. In the second paper of the (LRDs) 2 series, we present a systematic selection from DESI DR1 and identify 27 LRDs at z = 0.2–0.9, yielding a number density lower limit of 7.5 × 10 −10 cMpc −3 . We conducted near-IR spectroscopic follow-up observations for 21 of them, revealing their full spectral energy distribution (SED) shapes and emission lines. These low- z LRDs share the hallmark properties of their high- z counterparts: compact morphology, V-shaped UV-optical continua, broad Balmer emission with extreme decrements (median H α /H β ∼ 15), frequent Balmer absorption (70%), and blackbody-like optical-to-near-IR continua. All have low metallicity, occupy the same regions in the BPT diagram as high- z LRDs, and have softer ionizing spectra than typical AGNs. The consistency between low- z and high- z LRD properties indicates the same physical processes at work. The correlation between broad-line Balmer luminosity and L 5100 deviates from that of local type-1 AGNs, limiting the direct application of local BH mass calibrations. Ionized [O iii ] outflows are ubiquitous (78%). One LRD at z = 0.196, J1717+3807, shows robust long-term variability in the i and Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) bands. The optical-to-near-IR continua of LRDs reveal a wide range of temperatures ∼2000–4700 K (peak 0.6–1.4 μ m), with a subset showing cooler and larger envelopes than those at high z . Low- z LRDs serve not only as proximate laboratories for probing the nature of LRDs, but also trace the cosmic evolution of this population from the cosmic dawn to the present day.

picks.title: Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition
picks.abstract: Pharmacotherapies for obesity and type 2 diabetes are increasingly being evaluated for their effects on cognition and brain health. Evidence from preclinical models, observational cohorts, and clinical trials has intensified interest, but findings remain mixed. A central challenge is to determine whether potential cognitive effects arise from direct actions on neural circuits, indirect consequences of improved cardiometabolic health, or both. This Review examines the evidence across cardiometabolic disease, aging, and Alzheimer's disease, focusing on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)-based therapies and combination approaches that engage glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon, and amylin pathways. We assess how receptor pharmacology, brain exposure, metabolic context, and disease stage shape cognitive outcomes and discuss how mechanistic clarity could guide therapies aimed at preserving or improving cognition.

picks.title: Banana Split: Improved Cosmological Constraints with Two Light-curve-shape and Color Populations Using Union3.1+UNITY1.8
picks.abstract: Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) have been used to provide key constraints on the equation-of-state parameter of dark energy. They are generally standardized under the assumption that they belong to a single population, with luminosities standardized in a continuous (roughly linear) fashion using the observed light-curve timescale. We update the Union3+UNITY1.5 supernova (SN) cosmology analysis in light of increasing evidence for at least two core populations of SNe Ia and apply this “UNITY1.8” model to the updated “Union3.1” compilation. In addition to finding evidence for two different light-curve-shape ( x 1 ) distributions, we also find that the color distributions are different, that the light-curve-shape/magnitude standardization relations are different, and that these populations have different distributions across host-galaxy stellar mass and redshift. Importantly, we find that the residual host-mass–luminosity step found in prior SN Ia cosmology analyses is now consistent with zero for unreddened SNe. We report a significantly tightened constraint on the split in the red-color standardization between SNe in low- and high-mass galaxies. We find that the estimated uncertainties shrink on cosmological parameters when fitting the same SNe assuming two modes versus one mode. We confirm similar trends in simulated data when running both versions of Unified Nonlinear Inference for Type Ia cosmologY (UNITY) on the same (two-mode) simulations. For a flat ΛCDM cosmology, we find Ω m = 0.33 4 − 0.024 + 0.025 from SNe alone; for a flat w 0 – w a cosmology, we find w 0 = − 0.76 0 − 0.082 + 0.084 and w a = − 0.7 9 − 0.30 + 0.28 when including SNe, baryon acoustic oscillation, and cosmic microwave background. In the 2D w 0 – w a plane, UNITY1.8 decreases the tension with flat…

picks.title: Any-light-particle searches with ALPSII: First science results
picks.abstract: The light-shining-through-a-wall experiment ALPS II at DESY in Hamburg searched for axions and similar lightweight particles in its first science campaign from February to May 2024. No evidence for the existence of such particles was found. For pseudoscalar bosons like the axion, with masses below about 0.1 meV, we achieved a limit for the di-photon coupling strength of 1.5e-9 1/GeV at a 95% confidence level. This is more than a factor of 20 improvement compared to all previous similar experiments. We also provide limits on photon interactions for scalar, vector and tensor bosons. An achievement of this first science campaign is the demonstration of stable operation and robust calibration of the complex experiment. Currently, the optical system of ALPS II is being upgraded aiming for another two orders of magnitude sensitivity increase.

picks.title: Deploying liquid intelligence in cancer: Finding answers in our blood
picks.abstract: Liquid biopsies are one of the few noninvasive procedures for probing disease at the molecular level. They represent a scalable solution to cancer detection and monitoring by capturing tumor-derived signals from circulating biomolecules such as proteins, DNA, RNA, and metabolites. However, these signals are often sparse, heterogeneous, and shaped by genetics, demographics, and comorbidities. Recent advances in artificial intelligence, especially with multimodal foundation models, have proven capable of extracting signals from noisy, high-dimensional data. Pretraining on large cohorts and integrating complementary modalities may improve sensitivity for tumor signals in blood, though significant clinical and infrastructural barriers remain. This review synthesizes advances in liquid biopsy technologies and artificial intelligence and examines how their convergence can enable enhanced cancer monitoring.

picks.title: Cross-species multiomic atlas of the primate basal ganglia
picks.abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) are conserved brain regions essential for motor control, learning, emotion, and cognition and are implicated in neurological and psychiatric disease, yet a unified cross-species taxonomy of BG cell types is lacking. We present a multiomic consensus atlas of 1.8 million nuclei from humans, macaques, and marmosets spanning eight BG structures, integrating gene expression, open chromatin, and spatial profiling. Alignment across species and to mouse and human whole-brain atlases identifies 61 homologous cell types conserved over 76 million years. Dorsal-ventral spatial identity is more conserved than D1/D2 receptor or striosome/matrix identity, and striatum (STR) D2 SMYD2-HTR7 spiny projection neurons have distinct molecular, electrophysiological, and morphological features. Cis-regulatory analysis reveals conserved sequence grammars that encode cell identity and inform viral targeting, and cell-type-resolved mapping localizes psychiatric and neurodegenerative risk to specific BG cell populations. This work provides a foundational resource for BG evolution, function, and disease.

picks.title: "If we don't act now, someone will die" : temporal riskwork in action
picks.abstract: In this ethnographic study, we develop the concept of temporal riskwork -- actions taken to alter the temporal dynamics of risk -- by examining how riskworkers navigated situations of multiple dynamically evolving risks under severe time constraints. In such contexts, decisions about how and when to act are critically interdependent and made with attention to assessing urgencies, priorities and volatility of risk. Our study revealed how risk can present both synchronic and diachronic competing temporal demands, requiring temporally complex riskwork. We studied a mental health crisis team where actors collectively responded to clients’ urgent, often accelerating risks in high-stakes, time-pressured environments. We contribute to the literature by developing a model of temporal riskwork that explains how actors can collectively manage a set of ongoing risks by engaging in two connected temporal processes: decelerating synchronic risk momenta and redirecting diachronic risk trajectories. More generally, our model explains how riskworkers can collectively manage the temporal complexity of multiple concurrent risks, integrating their assessments and actions in complex, dynamic contexts.

more.title: Echoes of the Anthropocene: Noise pollution as a global threat
more.abstract: Anthropogenic noise is a rapidly expanding global pollutant, but its effects across biological levels from individuals to ecosystems remain unquantified. We conducted phylogenetically controlled meta-analyses of 214 experimental studies on 177 aquatic and terrestrial species with ranges that span six continents. Noise altered at least one physiological, developmental, or behavioral trait in 80% of species studied, with declines in fitness and abundance and disruptions of predator-prey interactions. Effects occurred in every habitat, although response mechanisms varied for some traits and species, creating winners and losers. Only multispecies analyses can reveal such species- and ecosystem-level impacts of anthropogenic stressors. Our results establish noise as a novel selection pressure reshaping ecosystem dynamics and as a pervasive stressor requiring soundscape protection alongside habitat conservation.

more.title: Quantitative measurement of viscosity in two-dimensional electron fluids
more.abstract: Electron hydrodynamics is an emerging framework that describes dynamics of interacting electron systems as conventional fluids. Although evidence for hydrodynamic-like transport has been reported in a variety of two-dimensional materials, precise quantitative measurement of the core parameter, electron viscosity, remains challenging. In this work, we demonstrate that magnetoresistance in Corbino-shaped graphene devices offers a simultaneous ohmmeter and viscosometer capability, allowing us to disentangle the individual ohmic and viscous contributions to transport, even near viscous-ohmic crossover. In both monolayer and bilayer graphene, the effective electron-electron scattering rate scales linearly with temperature, deviating markedly from the T 2 dependence expected in conventional Fermi liquids. Instead, it is consistent with a recently identified tomographic fluid regime, theoretically predicted to be generic for two-dimensional electron systems.

more.title: Preventing Malaria Infections and Moving toward Malaria Elimination
more.abstract: Malaria continues to be a major health challenge worldwide, causing an estimated 282 million cases of illness and 610,000 deaths in 2024, predominantly among African children. Despite recent stagnation in the progress of malaria prevention, the landscape is undergoing rapid transformation. This review examines current and emerging approaches to preventing malaria infection and supporting malaria elimination, including vector control, transmission-blocking interventions, chemoprevention, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines. Next-generation insecticide-treated nets, expanded use of seasonal malaria chemoprevention, and the introduction of RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M vaccines are already reshaping control strategies. Looking ahead, long-acting injectable chemoprevention, transmission-blocking medicines and vaccines, and improved surveillance-driven deployment may further accelerate progress. As funding becomes constrained and decision making shifts increasingly to countries where malaria is endemic, effective malaria prevention will depend on locally tailored, integrated combinations of interventions supported by strong surveillance, regulatory capacity, and national leadership.

more.title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
more.abstract: Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment 1–8 , suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear 9–13 . Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and…

more.title: Bouncing singularities in Schwarzschild geometry: A geometric origin of the quasinormal mode convergence region
more.abstract: We show analytically that the convergence of the QNM expansion of the retarded Green's function of the Schwarzschild spacetime is set by a singularity in the complex time plane. The singularity has a simple geometric origin: it is an example of a `bouncing singularity' in the language of AdS/CFT literature, caused by a null geodesic which bounces from the black hole singularity. Our work explains why the QNM convergence region at real times is bounded by null ray which scatters from the gravitational potential at a seemingly unremarkable point ($r_* = 0$ in the conventions of previous work) -- this ray is the same distance from the origin as the bouncing singularity in the relevant complex plane. The same set of singularities are responsible for an annular region of convergence for the Matsubara mode sum which describes the early time behaviour of the Schwarzschild Green's function for perturbations close to the horizon.

more.title: Obesity management medications: The way forward
more.abstract: Obesity is now widely recognized as a chronic progressive condition. The altered biological mechanisms that cause obesity frequently require long-term treatment, including pharmacotherapies or bariatric surgery. In recent decades, the pathophysiology of obesity has been understood to an extent that obesity management medication (OMM) discovery could be rationally pursued. Advances in defining the regulation of food intake and energy expenditure by molecular communication from peripheral organs to the brain led to the development of OMMs that appear capable of safely achieving scalable and sustained body weight loss. However, side effects, heterogeneous treatment responses, long-term metabolic adaptations, adherence, and other factors may limit the use of existing OMMs and justify the development of additional medications to improve the health of people living with obesity.

more.title: Equivalence of pseudogap and pairing energy in a cuprate high-temperature superconductor
more.abstract: The pseudogap stands out in the phase diagram of the cuprate high-temperature superconductors because its origin and relationship to superconductivity remain elusive. The origin of the pseudogap has been debated, with competing hypotheses attributing it to preformed electron pairs or local order, such as charge density waves. We present unambiguous evidence supporting the pairing scenario, using local shot-noise spectroscopy measurements in Bi 2 Sr 2 CaCu 2 O 8+δ . Our data demonstrate that the pseudogap energy coincides with the onset of electron pairing and is spatially heterogeneous with values reaching up to 70 milli–electron volts. Our results exclude a pure local order origin of the pseudogap, link the pseudogap to Cooper pair formation, and suggest that the limiting factor for higher critical temperature in cuprates is phase coherence.

more.title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia
more.abstract: Somatic evolution in ageing tissues underlies many cancers 1,2 . However, our quantitative understanding of the rules governing this pre-cancerous evolution remains incomplete. Here we exploit a unique collection of serial blood samples 3 , collected annually for up to a decade and beginning as early as 15 years before diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia, to provide a quantitative description of pre-cancerous evolutionary dynamics. Using deep duplex sequencing and evolutionary theory, we quantify the acquisition ages and fitness effects of the key driver events in acute myeloid leukaemia development. The first driver mutations are typically acquired in the first few decades of life, when the blood remains highly polyclonal. These early slow-growing clones subsequently acquire multiple further driver mutations that confer selective advantages up to 100-fold larger than the early drivers. These faster-growing clones harbouring multiple driver mutations can cause complete somatic sweeps of the blood decades before diagnosis, a feature strongly associated with future acute myeloid leukaemia. Our data show that the clonal dynamics of blood are consistent with a set of remarkably simple evolutionary rules that strike a balance between chance and determinism.

more.title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals molecular organization of human and nonhuman primate basal ganglia
more.abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) are interconnected subcortical nuclei with a complex topographical organization that orchestrate goal-directed behaviors and are implicated in neurodegenerative movement disorders. We generated a cellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics atlas of the BG in human, rhesus macaque, and common marmoset, sampling over one million cells in each species. By integrating spatial data with a cross-species consensus single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) cell-type taxonomy, this atlas reveals principles of molecular organization within and across structures. Extensive spatial sampling across the rostral-caudal axis illuminates complex, yet highly stereotyped, multi-axis gene expression gradients superimposed onto discrete compartments of the striatum. Additionally, we identify core-shell organization of the internal globus pallidus. This unified, cross-species spatial transcriptomics atlas will be a foundational resource for characterizing the molecular and functional organization of the BG and their roles in health and disease.

more.title: Anomaly to resource: The Mpemba effect in quantum thermometry
more.abstract: Quantum thermometry provides a key capability for nanoscale devices and quantum technologies, but most existing strategies rely on probes initialized near equilibrium. This equilibrium paradigm imposes intrinsic limitations: sensitivity is tied to long-time thermalization and often cannot be improved in fast, noisy, or nonstationary settings. In contrast, the \textit{Mpemba effect}, the counterintuitive phenomenon where hotter states relax faster than colder ones, has mostly been viewed as a thermodynamic anomaly. Here, we bridge this gap by proving that Mpemba-type inversions generically yield a finite-time enhancement of the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for temperature estimation, thereby converting an anomalous relaxation effect into a concrete metrological resource. Through explicit analyses of two-level and $Λ$-level probes coupled to bosonic baths, we show that nonequilibrium initializations can transiently outperform both equilibrium strategies and colder states, realizing a \emph{metrological Mpemba effect}. Our results establish anomalous relaxation as a general design principle for nonequilibrium quantum thermometry, enabling ultrafast and nanoscale sensing protocols that exploit, rather than avoid, transient dynamics.

more.title: Intravenous Thrombolysis for Acute Ischemic Stroke — New Directions
more.abstract: In the past 5 years, substantial changes have been made in the use of intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) in patients with acute ischemic stroke. Integrating IVT with endovascular thrombectomy, which improves outcomes in patients with stroke due to large cerebral vessel occlusion, has been a particular challenge. This review discusses the underlying vascular targets for IVT and thrombectomy, the increasing use of tenecteplase instead of alteplase, broadening indications for the use of IVT, and ancillary drugs and dosing methods that may augment the success of IVT.

more.title: Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion
more.abstract: Accessing reversible four-electron iodine redox chemistry in aqueous metal–iodine batteries offers a promising route towards high-energy aqueous energy storage, but has conventionally relied on highly concentrated, corrosive halogen-containing electrolytes to stabilize reactive hypervalent iodine cations through interhalogen complexation 1–9 . Here we show a kosmotropic anion–polar anion–nucleophilic species (Nuc) electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions, enabling reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes. Polar anions establish a water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment, whereas kosmotropic anions regulate water–Nuc interactions to increase the availability of Nuc for stabilizing hypervalent iodine cations through Nuc–I + –Nuc halogen bonds. This electrolyte framework is validated across diverse Nuc and in both aqueous Zn–I 2 and Al–I 2 batteries. Moving beyond conventional interhalogen stabilization, these findings establish a distinct electrolyte chemistry framework and represent a mechanistic shift for reversible multi-electron iodine chemistry in aqueous environments.

more.title: Eight New Ultramassive Black Hole Masses Confirm Best Correlation with Galaxy Core Sizes
more.abstract: We analyze black hole (BH) scaling relations at the high-mass end, focusing in particular on the regime of ultramassive black holes, M BH > 10 10 M ⊙ (UMBHs). Building on the new dynamical BH mass measurements presented in our companion paper for a sample of 16 brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs), including eight newly identified UMBHs based on triaxial Schwarzschild models, we investigate the implications of these measurements for BH scaling relations. This first sample of triaxial BH mass determinations increases the number of known UMBHs by a factor of 2 and dramatically increases the constraints for BH mass scaling relations at the high-mass end. We find that BCGs are outliers in the canonical M BH ∝ σ 4−5 relation, while the size of their depleted cores—the central light-deficient region—offers a tighter correlation with M BH with a scatter of 0.22 dex in this mass regime, confirming and extending earlier findings that core size provides a robust proxy at the high-mass end. Our measurements smoothly join the trend already established in previous studies. This also holds for tight correlations between core size and sphere-of-influence radius and core size and core density, which, along with the correlation between M BH and core size, strongly support the BH binary model for the formation of the centers of the most massive galaxies, as the observed core sizes are inconsistent with gravitational-wave recoil predictions and the galaxies display central tangential orbital anisotropy expected from scouring.

more.title: Conserved quantities enable the quantum Mpemba effect in weakly open systems
more.abstract: Observation of the quantum Mpemba effect has spurred much interest in its enabling conditions and its relation to the classical counterpart. Here, we consider weakly open many-body quantum systems initialized in different thermal states and examine when the initially farther state relaxes to the (non-equilibrium) steady state faster. We claim that the number of conserved quantities in the unitary part plays a crucial role: the Mpemba effect is possible only when the Hamiltonian commutes with other extensive operators or is integrable. The reason lies in the dynamical evolution happening in spaces of different dimensions. When energy is the only approximately conserved quantity, dissipation pushes the dynamics within a single-parameter manifold of different thermal states. In contrast, for Hamiltonians with several conserved quantities, the dynamics drift in the multi-dimensional space of generalized Gibbs ensembles, whose distance to the steady state is less trivial. We provide numerical results for large system sizes using tensor networks and free-fermion techniques, thereby supporting our claim.

more.title: Hyperbolic Large Language Models
more.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success and demonstrated superior performance across various tasks, including natural language processing (NLP), weather forecasting, biological protein folding, text generation, and solving mathematical problems. However, many real-world data exhibit highly non-Euclidean latent hierarchical anatomy, such as protein networks, transportation networks, financial networks, brain networks, and linguistic structures or syntactic trees in natural languages. Effectively learning intrinsic semantic entailment and hierarchical relationships from these raw, unstructured input data using LLMs remains an underexplored area. Due to its effectiveness in modeling tree-like hierarchical structures, hyperbolic geometry—a non-Euclidean space—has rapidly gained popularity as an expressive latent representation space for complex data modeling across domains such as graphs, images, languages, and multimodal data. Here, we provide a comprehensive and contextual exposition of recent advancements in LLMs that leverage hyperbolic geometry as a representation space to enhance semantic representation learning and multiscale reasoning. Specifically, the paper presents a taxonomy of the principal techniques of hyperbolic LLMs (HypLLMs) in terms of four main categories: (1) hyperbolic LLMs through exp/log maps; (2) hyperbolic fine-tuned models; (3) fully hyperbolic LLMs; and (4) hyperbolic state-space models. We also explore crucial potential applications and outline future research directions. A repository of key papers, models, datasets, and code implementations is available at https://github.com/sarangp2402/Hyperbolic-LLM-Models .

more.title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism
more.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD 1–3 . Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge 4 . Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in male than in female individuals 5 , and female autistic people tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared with their male counterparts 6,7 ; however, the biological basis of this ‘female protective effect’ (FPE) has remained unknown 8,9 . Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network enabled identification of central transcriptional regulators that drive this transcriptomic convergence, including prominent ASD gene CHD8 and candidates including REST . Furthermore, X-linked transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in female individuals 10 , emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in the female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the female protective effect. Together, these results show how key gene regulatory networks can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD.

more.title: On a conjecture of Almgren: area-minimizing submanifolds with fractal singular sets
more.abstract: We construct area-minimizing submanifolds with fractal singular sets on compact Riemannian manifolds. Thus, we settle a conjecture of Almgren, and our answer is sharp dimension-wise. Furthermore, we can prescribe arbitrarily the strata in the Almgren stratification of the singular sets of our area-minimizing submanifolds, and our results hold in the category of integral currents, mod v currents and stable stationary varifolds.

more.title: An Introduction to Computational Fluctuating Hydrodynamics
more.abstract: This short article is an introduction to the theory of fluctuating hydrodynamics (FHD) and the formulation of numerical schemes for the resulting stochastic partial differential equations. The stochastic heat equation (SHE) is derived, and simple finite-volume schemes for its solution are outlined. Numerical results from a Python program (see the supplementary materials ( supplement.pdf [ 196KB])) are shown to be in good agreement with theoretical solutions of the SHE for equilibrium and nonequilibrium systems. Finally, a menagerie of other FHD equations is outlined and suggested instructional exercises are listed.

more.title: Scalable generation of macroscopic Fock states exceeding 10,000 photons
more.abstract: The scalable preparation of bosonic quantum states with macroscopic excitations poses a fundamental challenge in quantum technologies, limited by control complexity and photon-loss rates that severely constrain prior theoretical and experimental efforts to merely dozens of excitations per mode. Here, based on the duality of the quantum state evolution in Fock state space and the optical wave-function propagation in a waveguide array, we introduce a Kerr-engineered multi-lens protocol in a single bosonic mode to deterministically generate Fock states exceeding $10,000$ photons. By optimizing phase and displacement operations across lens groups, our approach compensates for non-paraxial aberrations, achieving fidelities above $73\%$ in numerical simulations for photon numbers up to $N=100,000$. Counterintuitively, the protocol's execution time scales as $N^{-1/2}$ with the target photon number $N$, exhibiting robustness against the photon loss. Our framework enables exploration of quantum-to-classical transitions of giant Fock states, paving the way for advanced quantum metrology with significant quantum gains, and error-corrected quantum information processing in high-dimensional Hilbert spaces.

more.title: diffhydro : Inverse Multiphysics Modeling and Embedded Machine Learning in Astrophysical Flows
more.abstract: We present the extension of the differentiable hydrodynamics code, diffhydro , enabling scalable partial differential equation-constrained inference and integrated hybrid physics–machine learning (ML) models for a wide range of astrophysical applications. New physics additions include radiative heating/cooling, Ornstein–Uhlenbeck–driven turbulence, and self-gravity via multigrid Poisson. We demonstrate good agreement with the Athena++ code on standard validation tests like Sedov–Taylor, Kelvin–Helmholtz, and driven/decaying turbulence. We further introduce a solver-in-the-loop neural corrector that reduces coarse-grid errors during time integration while preserving stability. The addition of custom adjoints facilitates efficient end-to-end gradients and multidevice scaling. We present simulations up to 1024 3 elements, run on distributed GPU systems, and we show gradient-based reconstructions of complex initial conditions in turbulent, and self-gravitating, radiatively cooling flows. The code is written in JAX, and the solver’s modular finite-volume components are compiled by Accelerated Linear Algebra into fused accelerator kernels, delivering high-throughput forward runs and tractable differentiation through long integrations.

more.title: The Multiphase Circumgalactic Medium of DESI Emission-line Galaxies at z ∼ 1.5
more.abstract: We study the multiphase circumgalactic medium (CGM) of emission-line galaxies (ELGs) at z ∼ 1.5, traced by Mg II λ 2796, λ 2803 and C IV λ 1548, λ 1550 absorption lines, using approximately 8000 ELG-quasar pairs from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument. Our results show that both the mean rest equivalent width ( W 0 ) profiles and covering fractions of Mg II and C IV increase with ELG stellar mass at similar impact parameters, but show similar distributions when normalized by the virial radius. Moreover, warm C IV gas has a more extended distribution than cool Mg II gas. The dispersion of Mg II and C IV gas velocity offsets relative to the galaxy redshifts rises from ∼100 km s −1 within halos to ∼200 km s −1 beyond. We explore the relationships between Mg II and C IV W 0 and show that the two are not tightly coupled: at a fixed absorption strength of one species, the other varies by several-fold, indicating distinct kinematics between the gas phases traced by each. We measure the line ratios, Fe II /Mg II and C IV /Mg II , of strong Mg II absorbers and find that at <0.2 virial radius, the Fe II /Mg II ratio is elevated, while the C IV /Mg II ratio is suppressed compared with the measurements on larger scales, both with ∼4 σ significance. We argue that multiphase gas that is not cospatial is required to explain the observational results. Finally, by combining with the measurements in the literature, we show the redshift evolution of CGM properties and estimate the neutral hydrogen, metal, and dust masses in the CGM of DESI ELGs—found to be comparable to those in the interstellar medium.

more.title: Single-cell analysis of chromatin state and transcriptome in the human basal ganglia
more.abstract: The basal ganglia are central to motor control, learning, emotion, and reward processing, and their dysfunction contributes to many neurological and psychiatric disorders. Here, we generated a single-cell multi-omic atlas of histone modifications and transcriptomes across eight basal ganglia regions from neurotypical human donors. This atlas resolved cell-type- and region-specific landscapes of active and repressive candidate cis -regulatory elements and delineated gene regulatory networks underlying cell identity. We found that the combinatorial expression of homeobox transcription factors provides distinctive molecular descriptors of neuronal cell identities in the basal ganglia. Integration with matched MERFISH spatial transcriptomics further uncovered regional heterogeneity in epigenomic and transcriptional programs. Finally, we used this atlas to interpret noncoding risk variants associated with neuropsychiatric disorders and to construct a deep-learning model that predicts gene regulatory activities and variant effects. Together, this work provides a multimodal regulatory framework for understanding human basal ganglia organization, evolution, and disease genetics.

more.title: Multiscale spatial atlas of human basal ganglia cell types and communities
more.abstract: The human basal ganglia comprise functionally varied nuclei, but their cell-type composition and spatial organization have not been comprehensively resolved. We generated a multi-region, subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomic atlas by integrating multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH)+ and spatiotemporal enhanced-resolution omics sequencing (Stereo-seq) across four neurotypical donors. The datasets profiled ∼7.9 million cells across the caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens, and globus pallidus, resolving 60 transcriptionally distinct cell types. We identify region-selective molecular and spatial diversification of spiny projection neurons and non-neuronal populations. Subcellular RNA localization captures somatic size and projection-inferred signatures, reflecting direct- and indirect-pathway topology. Cellular community analyses reveal astrocyte and oligodendrocyte subclusters enriched at striosome-matrix borders, while primate-expanded interneurons are confined to matrix territories. Cross-species comparisons reveal conserved and species-specialized organization, including orthologous striosome-matrix architecture and conserved dorsolateral-to-ventromedial transcriptional gradients. Together, this multi-centimeter-scale human basal ganglia atlas links cell types, spatial architecture, and subcellular transcript topography across scales.

more.title: Industrialization drives convergent microbiome and host physiological shifts in the human metaorganism
more.abstract: Understanding how industrialization reshapes the human metaorganism requires integrating microbiome ecology with host physiology across globally diverse populations. Here, we generate multivariate data from the Global Microbiome Conservancy cohort, including gut microbiome, immunoglobulin A (IgA) sequencing, host genotyping, diet, lifestyle, and fecal biomarker profiles, to investigate host-microbiome interactions across gradients of industrialization and geography. We show that industrialization is associated with homogenized microbial compositions, reduced microbial diversity, and lower community stability, independent of host confounders. We further show that industrialization is linked to elevated markers of gut stress, increased IgA secretion, and altered patterns of IgA-bacteria interactions. Finally, we show that microbiome-based disease predictors trained on industrialized populations are uninformative in less industrialized cohorts, highlighting limited cross-population transferability. Together, our results reveal coordinated restructuring of the microbial ecosystem and host physiology and emphasize the need for inclusive, globally representative data to improve translational microbiome applications across diverse human populations.

more.title: Dwarf Galaxy Halo Masses from Spectroscopic and Photometric Lensing in DESI and DES
more.abstract: We present the most precise and lowest-mass weak lensing measurements of dwarf galaxies to date, enabled by spectroscopic lenses from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) and photometric lenses from the Dark Energy Survey (DES) calibrated with DESI redshifts. Using DESI spectroscopy from the first data release, we construct clean samples of galaxies with median stellar masses log 10 ( M * / M ⊙ ) =8.310.1 and measure their weak lensing signals with sources from DES, KiDS, and SDSS, achieving detections with signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) up to 12 for dwarf galaxies ( log 10 ( M * / M ⊙ ) < 9.25)—opening up a new regime for lensing measurements of low-mass systems. Leveraging DES photometry calibrated with DESI, we extend to a photometric dwarf sample of over 700,000 galaxies, enabling robust lensing detections of dwarf galaxies with combined S/N = 30 and a significant measurement down to log 10 ( M * / M ⊙ ) =8.0. The photometric sample is characterized using a self-organizing map calibrated with DESI spectroscopy, a methodology designed to scale to future surveys like Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s LSST where spectroscopic coverage will be relatively limited. We show that the one-halo regime (scales ≲0.15 h −1 Mpc) is insensitive to various systematic and sample selection effects, providing robust halo mass estimates, while the signal in the two-halo regime depends on galaxy color and environment. These results demonstrate that DESI already enables precise dwarf lensing measurements, and that calibrated photometric samples extend this capability. Together, they pave the way for novel constraints on dwarf galaxy formation and dark matter physics with upcoming surveys like LSST.

more.title: High-dimensional families of holomorphic curves and three-dimensional energy surfaces
more.abstract: Let $H: \mathbb{R}^4 \to \mathbb{R}$ be any smooth function. This article introduces some arguments for extracting dynamical information about the Hamiltonian flow of $H$ from high-dimensional families of closed holomorphic curves. We work in a very general setting, without imposing convexity or contact-type assumptions. For any compact regular level set $Y$, we prove that the Hamiltonian flow admits an infinite family of pairwise distinct, proper, compact invariant subsets whose union is dense in $Y$. This is a generalization of the Fish--Hofer theorem, which showed that $Y$ has at least one proper compact invariant subset. We then establish a global Le Calvez--Yoccoz property for almost every compact regular level set $Y$: any compact invariant subset containing all closed orbits is either equal to $Y$ or is not locally maximal. Next, we prove quantitative versions, in four dimensions, of the celebrated almost-existence theorem for Hamiltonian systems; such questions have been open for general Hamiltonians since the late 1980s. We prove that almost every compact regular level set of $H$ contains at least two closed orbits, a sharp lower bound. Under explicit and $C^\infty$-generic conditions on $H$, we prove almost-existence of infinitely many closed orbits.

more.title: 100 ± Δ t years of quantum uncertainty: From origins to modern insights
more.abstract: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle is a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, marking a decisive departure from classical physics. Conceived almost a century ago through a thought experiment showing that measuring an electron's position inevitably disturbs its momentum, it began as a deceptively simple idea that sparked countless studies and grew into the rich research field it is today. This review traces its development into a spectrum of mathematical formulations -- known as uncertainty relations -- and explores their interconnections and wide-ranging applications. We highlight its central role in quantum metrology, where it underpins strategies for extracting information from quantum systems with ever-increasing precision, and its links to multiparameter estimation and squeezed states. This review, dedicated to the centenary of the uncertainty principle, reflects on how it has deepened our understanding of quantum theory and driven practical advances, and looks ahead to a century poised for further surprising and transformative discoveries.

more.title: Inverse Design of Inorganic Compounds with Generative AI
more.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
more.abstract: Machine learning is revolutionizing chemistry. Beyond the value of predictive models accelerating virtual screening, generative AI aims at enabling inverse design, reversing the compound-to-property prediction paradigm into property-to-compound generation. Chemists now have access to a rich AI toolbox for organic chemistry, including drug discovery. However, the application of these methods to inorganic compounds remains limited by the challenges posed by their intrinsic nature. This perspective analyzes how these challenges have been addressed, considering widely diverse systems ranging from molecules to crystals, including transition metal complexes and microporous materials. The analysis focuses on how generative AI methods have evolved toward data-representation-model pipelines that address the full complexity of inorganic compounds, including their chemical composition, geometry, symmetry, and electronic structure. Future directions, like benchmark standardization and the development of synthesizability metrics, are also discussed.

more.title: Reconciling Discrete-Time Mixed Policies and Continuous-Time Relaxed Controls in Reinforcement Learning and Stochastic Control
more.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is currently one of the most prominent methods for optimizing dynamical systems, with breakthrough results across various fields. The framework is based on the concept of a Markov decision process (MDP), leading to a discrete-time optimal control problem. In the RL literature, such problems are typically formulated and solved using mixed policies, from which random actions are sampled at each time step. Recently, part of the optimal control community has begun investigating continuous-time versions of RL algorithms, replacing MDPs with continuous-time stochastic processes governed by relaxed controls and asserting a full analogy between the two formulations. In this work, we examine the limitations of this analogy and rigorously establish a connection between the two problems in the case where only the drift term of the continuous-time model is controlled. We prove strong convergence of the RL implementation of mixed strategies as the time discretization mesh tends to zero. We also discuss the technical challenges posed by the possible presence of control in the diffusion component of the state.

more.title: Colloquium: Semi-Dirac fermions in quantum matter
more.abstract: This article reviews the recent progress on the subject of semi-Dirac fermions, two dimensional quasiparticles that disperse quadratically, as Galilean invariant particles, or linearly, as massless relativistic particles, depending on their direction of motion. These particles exist at a phase boundary set by the continuous change in the connectivity of Fermi surfaces, known as topological Lifshitz transitions. The basic properties and the current experimental evidence of the existence of these particles in both synthetic lattices and quantum materials are presented. The many-body problem of semi-Dirac fermions is discussed from a theoretical perspective with an eye to physical observables of relevance to experiments.

more.title: Ambipolar Electrochemical Doping of CsPbBr 3 Nanocrystals
more.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
more.abstract: Electronic doping underpins many semiconductor applications but has remained elusive for lead halide perovskite nanocrystals because their high density and low formation energy of defects easily compensate introduced dopants. Here, we use electrochemical doping as a strategy to avoid doping compensation. Electrochemical injection of electrons or holes into the nanocrystal is compensated by surface-adsorbed electrolyte counterions, therefore not compromising crystal structure. We accomplished ambipolar (n- and p-type) doped CsPbBr3 nanocrystals with charge carrier concentrations ranging from intrinsic up to 4.8 × 1017 cm–3 (corresponding to 0.25 charges per nanocrystal). We show that electrochemical doping is reversible and stable at these free carrier concentrations. The extent of doping and stability are enabled by the use of lecithin, a zwitterionic ligand that strongly binds to the surface of the CsPbBr3 nanocrystals while still allowing ion and electron transfer. Lecithin stabilizes the surface atoms by shifting the potentials for Pb2+ reduction and Br– oxidation outside of the bandgap. The inferred surface-chemistry design rules for stable electrochemical doping can also serve as a guideline for developing CsPbBr3 nanocrystals stable under high free-carrier concentrations in optoelectronic devices, such as light-emitting diodes or electronically triggered quantum light sources.

more.title: Systemic Cyber Risk: Linking Measurement, Market Incentives, and Policy
more.abstract: Many firms and sectors within the global economy heavily depend on a common set of critical technology products and software services, thereby consolidating risk across a small number of potential failure points. The widespread reliance on a limited set of products and services has given rise to many single points of system vulnerability. Such concentration of risk amplifies the potential fallout from security breaches, especially since attackers have strong incentives to attack such products and services. Despite the abundance of tools available to organizations and consumers for safeguarding their data against loss or compromise, advancements in individual defense measures have been more than counterbalanced by an increased susceptibility to systemic events. In this paper, we apply economic principles to the rising danger of systemic cyber risks. The paper is organized around four central economic lessons and uses case studies, new data, and policy discussion to develop and support them.

more.title: Optical Access to a Molecular Nuclear-Spin Register in Catalytically Relevant Palladium(I) Complexes
more.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
more.abstract: Paramagnetic metal complexes are powerful tools in chemical catalysis and, increasingly, quantum information science, positioning them as ideal tools for quantum sensing within reactions themselves. However, this application requires an interface between spins and light in chemically relevant platforms. Here, we demonstrate that circularly polarized light can generate electron spin coherence in low-symmetry, catalytically relevant Pd(I) complexes. By measuring ultrafast changes in optical polarization with time-resolved Faraday rotation, we optically detect coherent superhyperfine interaction between the Pd(I)-centered electron spin and adjacent 31P nuclei from the ligand at ambient temperature in solution. The electronic origins of this behavior are attributed to excited-state orbital angular momentum through combined spectroscopic and computational analysis, and the optically measured coherence is benchmarked against pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance. Spin polarization is coherently exchanged between the electron spin and initially incoherent nuclear spins, constituting a rare example of optical access to a nuclear spin register in an ambient-temperature, solution-phase molecular system. Both reactivity and quantum spin function are mediated by the bisphosphine ligand; taken together with in situ detection of coherent Pd(I) spin dynamics directly in reaction mixtures, this work moves molecular qubits toward quantum sensing in chemical reactions.

more.title: Porphyrin-Driven Redox Tuning in Structurally Defined De Novo Heme Proteins
more.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
more.abstract: Designing redox proteins with predictable and tunable electron transfer properties is a major goal in de novo bioenergetics. Here we show that replacing heme B with a series of structurally conservative non-natural metalloporphyrins enables broad modulation of redox potentials over 400 mV in the de novo designed monoheme m4D2 and diheme 4D2 T19D. The non-natural porphyrins bind with high affinity and do not compromise either the heme binding site or global protein structure, as evidenced by X-ray crystallography and NMR spectroscopy. We also report the native-like NMR structure of m4D2 loaded with the non-natural and symmetric iron 2,4-dimethyldeuteroporphyrin IX, confirming our modular approach to tetrahelical redox protein design. This work establishes a versatile platform for constructing tunable electron carriers for engineered bioenergetic pathways and bioelectronic applications.

more.title: Channeled Attention and Stable Errors
more.abstract: People persist in mistaken beliefs even in settings with high stakes, abundant data, and repeated opportunities to learn—settings where standard arguments imply they should correct their errors. We develop an attention-based framework for understanding why errors persist. When a person channels his attention through the lens of his potentially misspecified model, exposure to data is not the same as tracking the statistics necessary to tell him his model is wrong. A model is attentionally stable when the data the person deems relevant will, in the long run, fail to make the model look implausible. Models that erroneously rule things out—e.g., beliefs that a variable doesn’t matter or that a distinction doesn’t exist—tend to be attentionally stable because they divert attention away from data that would refute the models. Conversely, models that erroneously rule things in are less likely to be stable. Whether an error is discovered depends on the structure of the decision problem but is not tightly linked to its level of harm; arbitrarily costly errors can persist while trivially inexpensive ones may be detected. Nevertheless, no error is robust both to changes in the decision environment and to shocks that expand attention: every channeled-attention error is vulnerable to some perturbation that would reveal it. We use the framework to analyze the stability of psychological biases and empirical misconceptions, as well as to explain why fresh eyes catch mistakes, why people use overly coarse rather than overly fine categorizations, and why people recognize errors in others that they miss in themselves.

more.title: TAVR in Patients with Moderate Aortic Stenosis with At-Risk Features
more.abstract: BACKGROUND: For patients with moderate aortic stenosis, current guidelines recommend clinical surveillance with echocardiographic assessment every 1 or 2 years. Whether transcatheter aortic-valve replacement (TAVR) will improve outcomes in these patients remains unknown. METHODS: We conducted an international, open-label, randomized trial to evaluate whether TAVR will result in better outcomes than clinical surveillance among patients with moderate aortic stenosis with at least one at-risk feature (i.e., a symptom or structural or functional abnormality that has been shown to be associated with faster disease progression or adverse cardiovascular outcomes). The patients were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to undergo transfemoral TAVR with a balloon-expandable valve or clinical surveillance. The primary effectiveness end point was a composite of death from any cause or a heart-failure event with or without hospitalization at 2 years. Superiority testing was performed in the intention-to-treat population. RESULTS: , and the mean aortic-valve peak velocity was 3.3 m per second. At 2 years, the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the percentage of patients with a primary effectiveness end-point event was 16.7% in the TAVR group and 23.9% in the clinical-surveillance group (risk difference, -7.2 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -13.1 to -1.3; P = 0.02 for superiority). The Kaplan-Meier estimate of the percentage of patients who died from any cause was 8.4% in the TAVR group and 7.3% in the clinical-surveillance group; the estimates for a heart-failure event were 10.8% and 19.0%, respectively. The incidence of procedure-related adverse events did not differ meaningfully between the patients in the TAVR group and those in the clinical-surveillance group who underwent aortic-valve…

more.title: Plozasiran for Severe Hypertriglyceridemia and Risk of Pancreatitis
more.abstract: BACKGROUND: messenger RNA, lowers triglyceride levels and potentially mitigates the risk of acute pancreatitis. METHODS: In two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, 757 adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive plozasiran (25 mg) or placebo at baseline and at months 3, 6, and 9. These trials had identical designs, end points, and analytic plans. The primary end point was the percent change in the fasting plasma triglyceride level from baseline to month 12. Key secondary end points were the percent change in the fasting triglyceride level from baseline to month 10, a fasting triglyceride level of less than 500 mg per deciliter (5.6 mmol per liter) and less than 150 mg per deciliter (1.7 mmol per liter), the percent change in the fasting serum triglyceride level at month 12 for patients with a baseline triglyceride level of 880 mg per deciliter or greater, and changes in remnant cholesterol and non-HDL cholesterol. A pooled analysis addressed adjudicated acute pancreatitis, incidence, and first-event timing. RESULTS: At month 12, patients in the plozasiran groups had a median triglyceride level that was lower than the baseline level by 79% and 81% in the two trials. These reductions corresponded to a median difference in the plozasiran groups as compared with the placebo groups (placebo-adjusted change) of -45 percentage points (95% confidence interval [CI], -51 to -38) and -47 percentage points (95% CI, -54 to -39). A triglyceride level of less than 500 mg per deciliter at 12 months was reported in 91% and 93% of the patients in the plozasiran groups and in 51% and 50% of those in the placebo groups (P<0.001). The rates of acute pancreatitis were 1 per 100 patient-years with plozasiran and 5 per 100 patient-years with…

more.title: Similarity Solutions of Shock Formation for First-Order Strictly Hyperbolic Systems
more.abstract: Shocks due to hyperbolic partial differential equations (PDEs) appear throughout mathematics and science. The canonical example is shock formation in the inviscid Burgers equation [Formula: see text]. Previous studies have shown that when shocks form for the inviscid Burgers equation, for positions and times close to the shock singularity, the dynamics are locally self-similar and universal, i.e., dynamics are equivalent regardless of the initial conditions. In this paper, we show that, in fact, shock formation is self-similar and universal for general first-order strictly hyperbolic PDEs in one spatial dimension, and the self-similarity is like that of the inviscid Burgers equation. An analytical formula is derived for the self-similar universal solution. Reproducibility of computational results. This paper has been awarded the “SIAM Reproducibility Badge: Code and data available” as a recognition that the authors have followed reproducibility principles valued by SIREV and the scientific computing community. Code and data that allow readers to reproduce the results in this paper are available at https://doi.org/10.34770/6vgh-br25 and in the supplementary materials ( M180373_SM.zip [25.7MB]). A higher dietary protein intake preserves fat-free mass during energy restriction-induced weight loss in individuals with overweight or obesity: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression
more.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
more.abstract: Background A higher dietary protein intake is often advocated to preserve fat-free mass during energy restriction-induced weight loss, yet the magnitude of effect in previous meta-analyses is highly variable. Objectives We aimed to determine the effects of a higher dietary protein intake on body composition during energy restriction-induced weight loss in individuals with overweight or obesity, with consideration for exercise, age, and protein difference. Methods We performed a systematic review to identify randomized controlled trials implementing higher or normal protein intakes alongside energy restriction-induced weight loss in individuals with overweight or obesity. Random-effects meta-analyses {mean difference [MD] [95% confidence intervals (CI)]} were performed for changes in fat-free mass and fat mass, respectively. Subgroup meta-analysis and meta-regression were performed to investigate potential modifiers of protein intake on fat-free mass changes. Results Thirty-three studies ( n = 2135) were included. A higher protein intake compared with a normal protein intake (mean ± standard deviation: 0.79 ± 0.11 compared with 1.25 ± 0.27 g⋅kg –1 ⋅d –1 ) preserved fat-free mass [MD (95% CI): 0.26 (0.04, 0.48) kg, P = 0.02, I 2 = 61%] and promoted greater fat mass loss [MD (95% CI): −0.69 (−0.95, −0.42) kg, P < 0.01, I 2 = 25%]. Subgroup meta-analysis found no effect of exercise compared with no exercise on fat-free mass ( P = 0.12). Exploratory analysis demonstrated exercise augmented fat-free mass preservation with a higher protein intake [MD (95% CI): 0.49 (0.14, 0.83) kg, P < 0.01]. However, this effect was only significant in younger (<60 y) adults [MD (95% CI): 0.60 (0.12, 1.09) kg, P = 0.01] and not in older (≥60 y) adults [MD (95% CI): 0.34 (−0.19, 0.87) kg, P…

shortlist.title: Differentiable Programming for Differential Equations: A Review
shortlist.abstract: The differentiable programming paradigm is a cornerstone of modern scientific computing. It refers to numerical methods for computing the gradient of a numerical model’s output. Many scientific models are based on differential equations, in which differentiable programming plays a crucial role in calculating model sensitivities, inverting model parameters, and training hybrid models that combine differential equations with data-driven approaches. Furthermore, recognizing the strong synergies between inverse methods and machine learning offers the opportunity to establish a coherent framework applicable to both fields. Differentiating functions based on the numerical solution of differential equations is nontrivial. Numerous methods based on a wide variety of paradigms have been proposed in the literature, each with pros and cons specific to the type of problem investigated. Here, we provide a comprehensive review of existing techniques to compute derivatives of numerical solutions of differential equations. We first discuss the importance of gradients of solutions of differential equations in a variety of scientific domains. Second, we lay out and compare the mathematical foundations of the various approaches. Third, we cover computational considerations and explore the solutions available in modern scientific software. Last but not least, we provide best practices and recommendations for practitioners. We hope that this work accelerates the fusion of scientific models and data and fosters a modern approach to scientific modeling.
