A higher dietary protein intake preserves fat-free mass during energy restriction-induced weight loss in individuals with overweight or obesity: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression
shortlist.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
shortlist.abstract: Background A higher dietary protein intake is often advocated to preserve fat-free mass during energy restriction-induced weight loss, yet the magnitude of effect in previous meta-analyses is highly variable. Objectives We aimed to determine the effects of a higher dietary protein intake on body composition during energy restriction-induced weight loss in individuals with overweight or obesity, with consideration for exercise, age, and protein difference. Methods We performed a systematic review to identify randomized controlled trials implementing higher or normal protein intakes alongside energy restriction-induced weight loss in individuals with overweight or obesity. Random-effects meta-analyses {mean difference [MD] [95% confidence intervals (CI)]} were performed for changes in fat-free mass and fat mass, respectively. Subgroup meta-analysis and meta-regression were performed to investigate potential modifiers of protein intake on fat-free mass changes. Results Thirty-three studies ( n = 2135) were included. A higher protein intake compared with a normal protein intake (mean ± standard deviation: 0.79 ± 0.11 compared with 1.25 ± 0.27 g⋅kg –1 ⋅d –1 ) preserved fat-free mass [MD (95% CI): 0.26 (0.04, 0.48) kg, P = 0.02, I 2 = 61%] and promoted greater fat mass loss [MD (95% CI): −0.69 (−0.95, −0.42) kg, P < 0.01, I 2 = 25%]. Subgroup meta-analysis found no effect of exercise compared with no exercise on fat-free mass ( P = 0.12). Exploratory analysis demonstrated exercise augmented fat-free mass preservation with a higher protein intake [MD (95% CI): 0.49 (0.14, 0.83) kg, P < 0.01]. However, this effect was only significant in younger (<60 y) adults [MD (95% CI): 0.60 (0.12, 1.09) kg, P = 0.01] and not in older (≥60 y) adults [MD (95% CI): 0.34 (−0.19, 0.87) kg, P…

shortlist.title: Named Reactions under Mechanochemical Conditions: A Critical Survey
shortlist.abstract: Mechanochemistry has progressed from a niche interest to a core method for solvent-free synthesis, providing sustainable and mechanistically unique alternatives to traditional solution-based chemistry. When controlled impact, shear, or vibrational energy is applied under solvent-free or solvent-lean conditions, reactions are promoted within dynamically renewed interfacial regions, revealing new patterns of selectivity, energy efficiency, and process design. This review surveys the historical development, fundamental principles, and analytical frameworks of mechanochemistry, together with an extensive compilation of named organic reactions conducted under mechanochemical conditions. By comparing mechanochemical reactions with their solution-phase counterparts, this review clarifies how stress-induced activation, microsolvation (η control), and auxiliary-mediated interfaces influence reaction kinetics, selectivity, and scalability. Emerging platforms, such as twin-screw extrusion (TSE), resonant acoustic mixing (RAM), and bead mills, extend these advantages toward scale-up and, in the case of TSE, continuous manufacturing, bridging laboratory-scale discoveries and industrial applications. Mechanochemistry functions both as a practical enabling platform and as a conceptual framework for Green Chemistry, embracing atom economy, solvent reduction, and operational safety within a unified solid-state synthetic framework.

shortlist.title: When Insurers Exit: Climate Losses, Fragile Insurers, and Mortgage Markets
shortlist.abstract: This paper uses a range of natural experiments to show how mispricing of climate risk in mortgages and property insurance creates large taxpayer exposures and leads to excess credit flows to risky areas. Our central finding is that the government-sponsored enterprises’ (GSEs) policies for evaluating property insurers are a crucial source of this mispricing. We assemble a comprehensive new dataset on both mortgages and insurance to analyze these dynamics in Florida from 2009-2018. We begin by documenting a breakdown in the quality of insurance provision, with new under-capitalized and under-diversified insurers dominating insurance markets. These fragile insurers have high rates of insolvency, which we show causally increases mortgage defaults after natural disasters. We find that the GSEs’ reliance on third-party ratings of insurers leads them to accept insurance from companies at high risk of insolvency without pricing for it. This creates large taxpayer exposures, with an estimated 25% of the GSEs’ expected losses in Florida coming from insurance fragility. Most starkly, we show that private lenders strategically respond to the GSE mispricing. Mortgage denial rates are sensitive to insurance quality in the jumbo segment where loans are retained, but not in the conforming segment where loans are offloaded to the GSEs. This suggests that, all else equal, fewer conforming mortgages would have been originated if lenders screened insurance fragility as they do in jumbos.

shortlist.title: Breathlessness mechanisms, measurement, and management in adults: evidence update on behalf of The Dyspnoea Society
shortlist.abstract: Breathlessness affects an estimated 40% of adults living with chronic disease, with substantial consequences for individuals, carers, and health-care systems. This Dyspnoea Society Research Statement, developed for researchers, clinicians, and adults living with or caring for someone with breathlessness, provides a state-of-the-art synthesis of recent advances in chronic breathlessness mechanisms, measurement, and management, and outlines a research agenda for the next decade. Key advancements include establishment of neural respiratory drive as a mechanistic contributor to exertional breathlessness; neuroimaging evidence that breathlessness arises from integration of peripheral and central processes within a dynamic brain network involving sensorimotor and cognitive-affective regions, supporting behavioural and psychosocial interventions; and improved measurement through responsive multidimensional instruments and approaches to quantify symptom abnormality relative to physical activity. Evidence supports early use of low-risk, non-pharmacological interventions for management of breathlessness, whereas evidence for pharmacological therapies is limited in most situations. Health-care redesign, including symptom-focused diagnostic pathways, integrated care models, and disease-agnostic breathlessness services, might help to improve patient outcomes while reducing health-care costs.

shortlist.title: "If we don't act now, someone will die" : temporal riskwork in action
shortlist.abstract: In this ethnographic study, we develop the concept of temporal riskwork -- actions taken to alter the temporal dynamics of risk -- by examining how riskworkers navigated situations of multiple dynamically evolving risks under severe time constraints. In such contexts, decisions about how and when to act are critically interdependent and made with attention to assessing urgencies, priorities and volatility of risk. Our study revealed how risk can present both synchronic and diachronic competing temporal demands, requiring temporally complex riskwork. We studied a mental health crisis team where actors collectively responded to clients’ urgent, often accelerating risks in high-stakes, time-pressured environments. We contribute to the literature by developing a model of temporal riskwork that explains how actors can collectively manage a set of ongoing risks by engaging in two connected temporal processes: decelerating synchronic risk momenta and redirecting diachronic risk trajectories. More generally, our model explains how riskworkers can collectively manage the temporal complexity of multiple concurrent risks, integrating their assessments and actions in complex, dynamic contexts.

shortlist.title: In Praise of the Bayesian Bootstrap
shortlist.abstract: The key takeaways from this article will be the following: (i) Anytime you can bootstrap, you should! (ii) Use the Bayesian bootstrap instead of the nonparametric bootstrap. (iii) If the bootstrap distribution looks different from the “theoretical” (usually, normal) distribution, don’t (only) report a point estimate and standard error. (iv) Instead (or in addition), report the bootstrap distribution with a plot if you have space for it or an interval if you don’t. (v) Give the Bayesian bootstrap a Bayesian interpretation. (vi) You can use a bootstrap even with (multiway) clustering.

shortlist.title: Reframing disease elimination: an update from the Lancet Commission on chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
shortlist.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with increasing global burden driven by population growth and ageing, persistent harmful exposures, and substantial health inequities. The Lancet Commission on COPD articulated an ambitious vision for disease elimination with prevention, early detection, and intervention. This Review revisits that vision, assesses progress since 2022, and calls for a broader commitment to lifelong lung health as an update of the Commission. Across seven sections, this Review advances a unified framework integrating the biology of lung development and ageing, precision medicine, patient-centred outcomes, and regulatory reform. COPD is not a single, uniform disease; rather, a biologically complex condition shaped by genetic, developmental, environmental, infectious, and behavioural factors across the entire life course. Effective prevention and care should therefore move beyond the detection and treatment of late physiological impairment toward earlier disease recognition, biological stratification, and interventions to preserve lung health, reduce symptoms, and prevent morbidity and premature mortality. The Review charts a path from reactive, late-stage management toward proactive, equitable, precision-based prevention and care. The central premise is unequivocal: the global burden of COPD can be substantially reduced. Success should be measured not only by gains in lung function and survival but also by improvements in daily functioning, quality of life, and wellbeing. In this expanded vision, COPD is no longer viewed solely as a chronic disease to be managed but as a preventable and modifiable condition within a broader commitment to lifelong lung health.

shortlist.title: Trends in the burden of diseases and their associations with multidimensional development among children and adolescents in China from 2000 to 2019: a retrospective analysis of a nationwide, repeated, cross-sectional survey
shortlist.abstract: BACKGROUND: Rapid social progress has transformed the health profile of Chinese children and adolescents, with declining diseases associated with poverty and rising diseases associated with wealth. This study aims to describe national trends in disease transitions and examine their associations with multidimensional provincial development. METHODS: In this retrospective study, we analysed data from the 2000, 2005, 2010, 2014, and 2019 waves of the nationwide, repeated, cross-sectional Chinese National Surveys on Students' Constitution and Health in Han Chinese children and adolescents aged 7-18 years from 30 provinces in mainland China. The survey used a multistage, stratified, cluster-sampling design with balanced distributions by age, sex, and residence (urban vs rural). Collected data were prevalences of diseases associated with wealth and development (overweight and obesity, dental caries, and visual impairment) and their coexistence (multimorbidity associated with wealth) in addition to diseases associated with poverty (undernutrition, anaemia, and Ascaris infestation), and their coexistence (multimorbidity associated with poverty). We integrated 13 provincial indicators reflecting economic, social, environmental, infrastructure, and innovation development to construct a Multidimensional Equality Development Index (MEDI) using an entropy method. To examine national trends in disease transitions and their associations with multidimensional development we used mixed-effects logistic regression and restricted cubic splines. Population-attributable fractions were estimated to describe how development domains related to disease patterns. FINDINGS: The study included 1 085 072 participants across five survey waves. Between 2000 and 2019, nationally, the prevalence of…

shortlist.title: Private Credit, Balance Sheets, and Financial Stability
shortlist.abstract: Private credit has become an important source of business financing, raising questions about financial stability. We examine these questions using comprehensive fund- and asset-level data on private credit funds, the dominant form of private credit. Four facts emerge. First, private credit funds are primarily equity financed, with equity accounting for 65–80 percent of assets, compared with about 10 percent for US banks. Second, they engage in little maturity transformation: Fund lives span eight to twelve years, while underlying loans typically mature within two to four years. Third, portfolios are diversified across industries, geographies, and credit strategies. Fourth, equity investors have earned average net annualized returns of about 10 percent after fees, with equity cushions historically absorbing losses before creditors. These findings suggest that private credit funds do not currently replicate balance-sheet structures associated with banking fragility. We conclude by discussing potential vulnerabilities related to liquidity provision, valuation contagion, and loss transmission through investor balance sheets.

shortlist.title: Can Government Support for Innovation Create the Next Silicon Valley?
shortlist.abstract: Can government support for innovation create the next Silicon Valley? We examine what public research and development can and cannot do to foster regional knowledge hubs. The historical record suggests that many successful hubs owe their origins partly to serendipity and favorable initial conditions. We then review causal evidence from universities, changes in intellectual property rules, new research institutions, wartime R&D, and the space race. Public R&D can raise local innovation, employment, and income, but the effects are heterogeneous, often modest relative to cost, and may partly reflect the relocation of firms and skilled workers from elsewhere. The evidence suggests a central role for complementary local inputs, including entrepreneurs, risk capital, skilled labor, firms, and institutions. Public R&D can help build a hub, but is unlikely to create one on its own.

shortlist.title: Abstract 13530: Factor XI/XIa Inhibitors for Secondary Prevention After Non-Cardioembolic Ischemic Stroke and High-Risk Transient Ischemic Attack: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
shortlist.abstract: Background: Factor XI/Xia inhibitors have gained attention as an innovative anticoagulant strategy which may reduce thrombosis without substantially impairing hemostasis. Their role in secondary prevention following non-cardioembolic stroke and high-risk transient ischemic attack (TIA) remains uncertain. We conducted an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trial (RCTs) assessing the efficacy and safety of factor XI/Xia inhibition in patient with these conditions. Research Question: Does treatment with factor XI/XIa inhibitors improve clinical outcomes while minimizing bleeding complications compared with conventional therapy in patients with non-cardioembolic stroke or high-risk TIA? Methods: A thorough search was performed on PubMed, Scopus, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov and the Cochrane library from inception until May 2025 comparing Factor XI/XIa inhibitors, primarily asundexian and milvexian, with placebo or standard antithrombotic therapy in patients with non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA. Pooled Risk Ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were computed using random-effects models. Results: Five RCTs involving 18,603 participants were included. Factor XI/XIa inhibitors were associated with a significant reduction in symptomatic ischemic stroke compared with control therapy (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.68-0.86; p<0.00001; I 2 =0%). No significant differences were observed for the composite of symptomatic ischemic stroke and covert infarction (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.87-1.18; p=0.89; I 2 =0%) or the composite of symptomatic ischemic stroke and TIA (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.61-1.01; p=0.06; I 2 =0%). Similarly, Factor XI/XIa inhibition did not significantly affect major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.78-1.10;…

shortlist.title: The commutativity problem for effective varieties of formal series, and applications
shortlist.abstract: A formal series in noncommuting variables Σ over the rationals is a mapping \(\Sigma ^* \rightarrow {\mathbb {Q}} \) from the free monoid generated by Σ to the rationals. We say that it is commutative if the output does not depend on the order of the symbols in the input. The commutativity problem for a class of series takes as input a (finite presentation of) a series from the class and amounts to establishing whether it is commutative. This is a very natural, albeit nontrivial problem, which has not been considered before from an algorithmic perspective. We show that commutativity is decidable for all classes of series that constitute a so-called effective prevariety , a notion generalising Reutenauer’s varieties of formal series. For example, the class of rational series , introduced by Schützenberger in the 1960’s, is well-known to be an effective (pre)variety, and thus commutativity is decidable for it. In order to showcase the applicability of our result, we consider classes of formal series generalising the rational ones. We consider polynomial automata , shuffle automata , and infiltration automata , and we show that each of these models recognises an effective prevariety of formal series. Consequently, their commutativity problem is decidable, which is a novel result. We find it remarkable that commutativity can be decided in a uniform way for such disparate computation models. Finally, we present applications of commutativity outside the theory of formal series. We show that we can decide solvability in sequences and in power series for restricted classes of algebraic difference and differential equations, for which such problems are undecidable in full generality. Thanks to this, we can prove that the syntaxes of multivariate polynomial recursive sequences…

shortlist.title: Abstract 15126: Elective Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump Ranks Highest for Survival in High-Risk Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials
shortlist.abstract: Background: The optimal mechanical circulatory support strategy for patients undergoing high-risk percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains uncertain. Randomized trials evaluating elective intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP), Impella, and standard care have reported conflicting results and have not been synthesized within a unified comparative framework. Research Question/Hypothesis: We evaluated the comparative efficacy and safety of elective IABP, Impella, and standard care in planned high-risk PCI. Methods: We systematically identified randomized controlled trials enrolling patients with severe left ventricular dysfunction undergoing planned high-risk PCI. A Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis compared elective IABP, Impella, and standard care. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included periprocedural myocardial injury, major bleeding, vascular complications, spontaneous myocardial infarction, and stroke. Results: Three randomized trials (BCIS-1, PROTECT II, and CHIP-BCIS3) comprising 1,053 patients formed a closed triangular evidence network. Model convergence was excellent (all R̂<1.01), with low estimated between-study heterogeneity (posterior median τ=0.346). For all-cause mortality, elective IABP demonstrated the most favorable treatment profile. Compared with standard care, IABP was associated with a 40% reduction in mortality odds (OR 0.60, 95% CrI 0.24-1.31) and an 89.7% posterior probability of benefit. This signal remained consistent across prespecified sensitivity analyses, including long-term follow-up data (OR 0.64, 95% CrI 0.29-1.30; probability of benefit 91.4%). Impella was associated with a directionally unfavorable mortality profile compared with standard care (OR 1.14, 95% CrI 0.47-2.24), with a 63.7%…

shortlist.title: Harnessing Contact Electrification and Static Charge for Chemical Reactions: Fundamentals and Applications of Contact Electrocatalysis
shortlist.abstract: The chemical industry is the largest industrial energy consumer and the third-largest emitter of CO2 globally. Despite efforts to enhance energy efficiency, many chemical reactions still require significant external energy due to fundamental thermodynamic barriers. Thus, transitioning to a sustainable chemical industry requires new renewable energy or catalytic technologies that reduce energy demand. In catalytic systems, flowing liquids, moving parts, and gas separation mean local static charge is often generated on the nanoscale. This review explores the static charge formation at solid–solid, solid–liquid, and solid–gas interfaces, such as those that occur in catalytic reactions, and then extends this discussion to a deeper focus on how these generated static charges can be used for catalysis, including electrostatic catalysis, static charge electrochemistry, and contact electrocatalysis (CEC). CEC, where motion-induced charge separation leads to local static charge formation, is then specifically examined, exploring why and how it has emerged as an exciting tool to enable these green chemical transformations. The focus is to highlight the most recent developments in CEC, with mechanistic interpretation, factors that affect CEC performance, and emerging applications, and to provide outlook and guidance for the field─specifically highlighting the need to build structure–property relationships for CEC performance and static charge formation for target chemical reactions.
shortlist.topic: Advanced Sensor and Energy Harvesting Materials

shortlist.title: Transition-Metal-Catalyzed Multicomponent Cycloadditions
shortlist.abstract: Transition-metal-catalyzed multicomponent cycloadditions provide a powerful strategy for constructing complex cyclic frameworks from simple unsaturated building blocks with high atom and step efficiencies. This Review highlights the progress made in transition-metal-catalyzed multicomponent cycloadditions based on the size of the cyclic products formed. First, reactions that construct five-membered rings, including [2 + 2 + 1], [3 + 1 + 1], and [2 + 1 + 1 + 1] cycloadditions, are discussed with an emphasis on key reactive intermediates, such as carbon monoxide, vinylidenes, carbenoids, and nitrenes. Next, six-membered-ring-forming processes, particularly [2 + 2 + 2], [3 + 2 + 1], [4 + 1 + 1], and [2 + 1 + 2 + 1] cycloadditions, are described, highlighting combinations of alkynes, alkenes, and heteroatom-containing components. The Review then covers strategies for constructing seven-membered rings via [3 + 2 + 2] and [4 + 2 + 1] cycloadditions. Finally, emerging methods that enable the formation of eight- and nine-membered rings through higher-order multicomponent cycloadditions are described. This Review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the conceptual framework, mechanistic principles, and synthetic possibilities of transition-metal-catalyzed multicomponent cycloadditions by organizing them according to ring size and cycloaddition components.

shortlist.title: Efficient and accurate mixed model association tool for single-cell eQTL analysis
shortlist.abstract: Genetic effects on gene expression often vary across cell types, motivating expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) mapping in single-cell RNA sequencing data. Existing approaches generally aggregate expression across cells, use Gaussian models poorly suited to read counts or do not scale. Here we show that SAIGE-QTL, a Poisson mixed model that directly models single-cell read counts, enables calibrated and computationally scalable eQTL mapping while accounting for donor-level and cell-level covariates and unequal numbers of cells per donor. In simulations and three single-cell datasets, SAIGE-QTL improved statistical efficiency and discovery of genes with significant eQTLs (eGenes) relative to pseudobulk methods and produced results consistent with existing single-cell models at substantially lower computational cost. In 1.2 million immune cells, SAIGE-QTL identified 48.8% more eGenes than pseudobulk analysis. SAIGE-QTL further enabled genome-wide trans-eQTL mapping and rare variant set-based testing, identifying rare variant associations independent of common eQTL signals. SAIGE-QTL therefore expands single-cell eQTL discovery across common, rare and trans-acting genetic variation.

shortlist.title: Diffusion Models for Small-Molecule Design
shortlist.abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have emerged as a class of generative models for controllable small-molecule design in drug discovery capable of progressively transforming noisy or partially specified molecular states into candidate structures under structural, geometric, and property constraints. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of the methodological foundations and representative applications of diffusion-based molecular generation, emphasizing the alignment among molecular representations, generative dynamics, controllable design, and evaluation and validation. Particular attention is given to recent advances in property- and structure-guided generation, target-aware and fragment-based design, multiobjective optimization, and synthesis-aware generation. We also discuss the roles of data sets, computational evaluation, and prospective experiments in assessing the chemical and biological relevance of generated molecules. By organizing these developments within a unified conceptual framework, we provide computational chemists and drug discovery researchers with a structured roadmap that balances the mathematical rigor with chemical intuition. Throughout, we highlight current methodological limitations and unresolved challenges and conclude with future directions toward chemically credible and experimentally grounded molecular design. To facilitate navigation of this rapidly evolving field, we introduce an interactive companion platform (https://diffsmd.scbdd.com) that provides a curated, continuously updated repository of model architectures and visualizations.

shortlist.title: Participatory Budgeting in Public Health: Promise, Evidence, Challenges, and Opportunities
shortlist.abstract: Participatory budgeting (PB) is a deliberative decision-making process that invites community participation to direct spending for a defined portion of public budgets. Originating in Brazil in the 1980s, PB has since diffused across the globe, including several hundred cases in the United States and Canada alone. PB programs vary but are generally characterized by five core principles: voice, vote, social inclusion, social justice, and oversight. Research on PB shows promising though moderate associations with improved population health outcomes, including infant mortality reductions and health and sanitation spending increases. Despite PB's conceptual alignment with many public health values, adoption of PB by US public health agencies remains limited, constrained by categorical funding requirements, small discretionary budgets, and a polarized sociopolitical environment. This article reviews PB's conceptual foundations, evidence base, and real-world applications before examining structural and political challenges and opportunities for PB as a means to improve the public's health.

shortlist.title: Proximal redox coupling enables oxidation damping for stable water electrolysis
shortlist.abstract: The design of atomically precise catalysts requires strategies that regulate their electronic and structural dynamics under operating conditions. While conventional doping can effectively tune bulk materials, it translates poorly to single-atom catalysts (SACs), in which isolated atoms lack extended coordination and are prone to oxidative instability. Here we design atomically dispersed Ru−O−Cr motifs that enable oxidation damping during acidic oxygen evolution. In situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy shows attenuated Ru oxidation synchronized with anticorrelated and partially reversible Cr redox evolution, consistent with proximity-dependent redox coupling. This buffered redox response is accompanied by bounded and partially reversible changes in the local metal−oxygen coordination environment. These coupled dynamics support proximity-coupled Ru−O−Cr redox units, enabling a 55.7-fold increased resistance against oxidation-induced Ru dissolution compared with conventional SACs. In proton exchange membrane water electrolysis, catalysts incorporating proximal Ru−O−Cr configurations exhibit degradation rates that are 6.8-fold and 14.4-fold lower than those of Ru SACs and commercial RuO2, respectively, at 1 A cm−2. These results suggest proximal oxidation damping as a potential design principle for stabilizing atomically precise electrocatalysts. Single-atom catalysts can mitigate reliance on scarce noble metals, but isolated sites can be fragile. Here a catalyst with proximal Ru−O−Cr motifs is fabricated that demonstrates proximal oxidation damping where the Cr neighbour buffers Ru overoxidation, improving stability for acidic oxygen evolution.

shortlist.title: Optimal learning of quantum channels in diamond distance
shortlist.abstract: The evolution of quantum states can be described by quantum channels. The task of estimating an unknown quantum channel, known as process tomography, is a central problem in quantum information theory. A long-standing open question is how many uses of an unknown channel are required to learn it to a precision quantified by the standard metric for distinguishing quantum processes, known as the diamond distance. Here we address this by establishing the query complexity of channel tomography with optimal dependence on the dimensions of the input and output spaces and the channel’s Kraus rank at any fixed constant accuracy in diamond distance. We design an algorithm that establishes an upper bound and prove a matching lower bound for learning a channel to the given accuracy. Our algorithm follows the strategy of performing optimal tomography on the Choi-state representation of the process, and we show that channel tomography can be reduced to the well-studied problem of pure-state tomography. As channels subsume states, unitaries and measurements as special cases, our protocol provides a unified framework for tomography of these tasks.

fundamentals.title: Operator structure of power corrections and anomalous scaling in energy correlators
fundamentals.abstract: Energy correlators offer a clean probe of quantum chromodynamics, serving as an ideal laboratory to rigorously investigate non-perturbative power corrections. The recent discovery that linear corrections exhibit a universal anomalous scaling points to a deep, underlying theoretical structure. We uncover the quantum field-theoretic origin of this phenomenon in the energy-energy correlator using light-ray operators. Through an explicit loop calculation, we derive the one-loop anomalous dimension, revealing that the dijet operator must be combined with a specific triple-jet component. This provides a first-principles framework that connects operator theory with high-precision collider phenomenology.
fundamentals.topic: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

fundamentals.title: Unified theory of quartz tuning fork resonators
fundamentals.abstract: Quartz tuning forks, functioning as electrically driven piezoelectric resonators, have long served as exceptionally stable and widely adopted timing references in diverse domains of research and industry. Yet, experimentally measured electrical resonance spectra often exhibit resonance evolutions that remain unexplained within existing theoretical descriptions. Here we develop a unified continuum electromechanical modal framework that integrates piezoelectric electrodynamics, variational structural dynamics, and symmetry-selected electromechanical observability. Our theory shows quantitative agreement with experimental results, demonstrating that electrical observability emerges not from the underlying mechanical eigenmodes alone. The resulting framework unifies conventional coupled-oscillator, equivalent-circuit, and continuum descriptions within a single first-principles theory and provides a rigorous basis for precision electromechanical characterization.

fundamentals.title: Phase transition in a dryland shrub–grass ecosystem: Emergence through local trade-offs
fundamentals.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
fundamentals.abstract: Ecosystems are complex adaptive systems in which local interactions among individuals shape macroscopic phenomena such as pattern formation, multistability, and critical transitions. However, how such bottom-up interactions govern emergent behaviors and system-level complexity remains a central challenge in ecology. Phase transition theory, a classic paradigm in physics, links local interaction rules to emergent changes in macroscopic system states, offering a formal language for understanding cross-scale dynamics. Here we unite this theory with empirical evidence from dryland shrub-grass ecosystems and show that these systems exhibit three hallmarks of phase transitions. First, abrupt shifts separate different phases of deserts, shrublands, and grasslands. Second, shrublands and grasslands self-organize into Turing-like phase patterns, contrasting with homogeneous deserts. Third, special phenomena emerge near-transition threshold, including patch enlargement and abrupt decline at desert-vegetation interface, and fairy circles within the shrub-grass transition zone. Using a cellular automaton model built on a fundamental trade-off between extensive and intensive resource foraging strategies (EI trade-off), we show how kernels encoding local trade-offs integrate these seemingly disparate phenomena within a unified phase transition framework. Moreover, this EI trade-off was empirically validated through analyses of plant functional traits and spatial patterns of plant patches. These findings illustrate that dryland ecosystem dynamics reflect universal self-organization principles. Our work establishes phase-transition theory as a powerful framework for understanding, predicting, and managing complexity in dryland ecosystems, which advances the integration of complexity…

fundamentals.title: The Gopakumar--Vafa finiteness conjecture
fundamentals.abstract: The Gopakumar--Vafa conjecture predicts that the BPS invariants of a symplectic 6-manifold, defined in terms of the Gromov--Witten invariants, are integers and all but finitely many vanish in every homology class. The integrality part of this conjecture was proved earlier by Ionel and Parker. This article proves the finiteness part. The proof relies on a modification of Ionel and Parker's cluster formalism using results from geometric measure theory.

fundamentals.title: Microscopic theory of phonon polaritons and long-wavelength dielectric response
fundamentals.abstract: We present a first-principles approach for calculating phonon-polariton dispersion relations. In this approach, phonon-photon interaction is described by quantization of a Hamiltonian that describes harmonic lattice vibrations coupled with the electromagnetic field inside the material. All Hamiltonian parameters are obtained from first-principles calculations, with diagonalization leading to non-interacting polariton quasiparticles. This method naturally includes retardation effects and resolves non-analytical behavior and ambiguities in phonon frequencies at the Brillouin zone center, especially in non-cubic and optically anisotropic materials. Furthermore, by incorporating higher-order terms in the Hamiltonian, we also account for quasiparticle interactions and spectral broadening. Specifically, we show how anharmonic effects in phonon polaritons lead to a dielectric response that challenges traditional models. The accuracy and consequences of the approach are demonstrated on GaP and GaN as harmonic test systems and PbTe and $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ as anharmonic test systems.

The task of estimating an unknown quantum channel, known as process tomography, is a central problem in quantum information theory. A long-standing open question is how many uses of an unknown channel are required to learn it to a precision quantified by the standard metric for distinguishing quantum processes, known as the diamond distance. Here we address this by establishing the query complexity of channel tomography with optimal dependence on the dimensions of the input and output spaces and the channel’s Kraus rank at any fixed constant accuracy in diamond distance. We design an algorithm that establishes an upper bound and prove a matching lower bound for learning a channel to the given accuracy. Our algorithm follows the strategy of performing optimal tomography on the Choi-state representation of the process, and we show that channel tomography can be reduced to the well-studied problem of pure-state tomography. As channels subsume states, unitaries and measurements as special cases, our protocol provides a unified framework for tomography of these tasks.

fundamentals.title: Sound propagation in striped supersolid gases at zero temperature
fundamentals.abstract: The role of dimensionality in the identification of sound modes in many-body systems characterized by the spontaneous breaking of translational symmetry is a topic of high interdisciplinary interest in both classical and quantum systems. The emergence of stripes in superfluids is a particularly interesting example where the dimensionality of the system differs from the one of the crystal phase. Here we present a unified hydrodynamic approach for the sound propagation in the stripe phase realized in ultracold dipolar and spin-orbit-coupled Bose gases at zero temperature. Despite the deep difference of the two platforms at a microscopic level, a similar hydrodynamic description can be formulated at a macroscopic level. The main difference between the two platforms is the lack of Galilean invariance in the spin-orbit case, resulting in a different identification of the normal (non-superfluid) component of the density. In both cases the spectrum comprises two sounds, reflecting the spontaneous breaking of the U(1) and translational symmetries. Both sounds exhibit an anisotropic behavior. A comparison with the first and second sounds of the smectic-A liquid crystal is also presented.
fundamentals.topic: Cold Atom Physics and Bose-Einstein Condensates

fundamentals.title: High-dimensional families of holomorphic curves and three-dimensional energy surfaces
fundamentals.abstract: Let $H: \mathbb{R}^4 \to \mathbb{R}$ be any smooth function. This article introduces some arguments for extracting dynamical information about the Hamiltonian flow of $H$ from high-dimensional families of closed holomorphic curves. We work in a very general setting, without imposing convexity or contact-type assumptions. For any compact regular level set $Y$, we prove that the Hamiltonian flow admits an infinite family of pairwise distinct, proper, compact invariant subsets whose union is dense in $Y$. This is a generalization of the Fish--Hofer theorem, which showed that $Y$ has at least one proper compact invariant subset. We then establish a global Le Calvez--Yoccoz property for almost every compact regular level set $Y$: any compact invariant subset containing all closed orbits is either equal to $Y$ or is not locally maximal. Next, we prove quantitative versions, in four dimensions, of the celebrated almost-existence theorem for Hamiltonian systems; such questions have been open for general Hamiltonians since the late 1980s. We prove that almost every compact regular level set of $H$ contains at least two closed orbits, a sharp lower bound. Under explicit and $C^\infty$-generic conditions on $H$, we prove almost-existence of infinitely many closed orbits.

fundamentals.title: The Huang–Yang conjecture for the low-density Fermi gas
fundamentals.abstract: Our work establishes a three-term asymptotic expansion of the ground state energy of a dilute gas of spin $1/2$ 1 / 2 fermions with repulsive short-range interactions, validating a formula predicted by Huang and Yang in 1957. The formula is universal in the sense that it holds for a large class of interaction potentials and depends on those only via their scattering length. We have recently proved an upper bound on the ground state energy of the desired form, and the present work completes the program by proving the matching lower bound.

fundamentals.title: Similarity Solutions of Shock Formation for First-Order Strictly Hyperbolic Systems
fundamentals.abstract: Shocks due to hyperbolic partial differential equations (PDEs) appear throughout mathematics and science. The canonical example is shock formation in the inviscid Burgers equation [Formula: see text]. Previous studies have shown that when shocks form for the inviscid Burgers equation, for positions and times close to the shock singularity, the dynamics are locally self-similar and universal, i.e., dynamics are equivalent regardless of the initial conditions. In this paper, we show that, in fact, shock formation is self-similar and universal for general first-order strictly hyperbolic PDEs in one spatial dimension, and the self-similarity is like that of the inviscid Burgers equation. An analytical formula is derived for the self-similar universal solution. Reproducibility of computational results. This paper has been awarded the “SIAM Reproducibility Badge: Code and data available” as a recognition that the authors have followed reproducibility principles valued by SIREV and the scientific computing community. Code and data that allow readers to reproduce the results in this paper are available at https://doi.org/10.34770/6vgh-br25 and in the supplementary materials ( M180373_SM.zip [25.7MB]). fundamentals.title: Named Reactions under Mechanochemical Conditions: A Critical Survey
fundamentals.abstract: Mechanochemistry has progressed from a niche interest to a core method for solvent-free synthesis, providing sustainable and mechanistically unique alternatives to traditional solution-based chemistry. When controlled impact, shear, or vibrational energy is applied under solvent-free or solvent-lean conditions, reactions are promoted within dynamically renewed interfacial regions, revealing new patterns of selectivity, energy efficiency, and process design. This review surveys the historical development, fundamental principles, and analytical frameworks of mechanochemistry, together with an extensive compilation of named organic reactions conducted under mechanochemical conditions. By comparing mechanochemical reactions with their solution-phase counterparts, this review clarifies how stress-induced activation, microsolvation (η control), and auxiliary-mediated interfaces influence reaction kinetics, selectivity, and scalability. Emerging platforms, such as twin-screw extrusion (TSE), resonant acoustic mixing (RAM), and bead mills, extend these advantages toward scale-up and, in the case of TSE, continuous manufacturing, bridging laboratory-scale discoveries and industrial applications. Mechanochemistry functions both as a practical enabling platform and as a conceptual framework for Green Chemistry, embracing atom economy, solvent reduction, and operational safety within a unified solid-state synthetic framework.

fundamentals.title: On a conjecture of Almgren: area-minimizing submanifolds with fractal singular sets
fundamentals.abstract: We construct area-minimizing submanifolds with fractal singular sets on compact Riemannian manifolds. Thus, we settle a conjecture of Almgren, and our answer is sharp dimension-wise. Furthermore, we can prescribe arbitrarily the strata in the Almgren stratification of the singular sets of our area-minimizing submanifolds, and our results hold in the category of integral currents, mod v currents and stable stationary varifolds.

fundamentals.title: Linear scaling reveals low-dimensional structure in observable microbial dynamics
fundamentals.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
fundamentals.abstract: Microbial communities often exhibit apparently complex dynamics driven by myriad interactions among community members and with their environments. Yet, practical modeling and control are often based on a limited number of observables, raising fundamental questions: are these observed dynamics low-dimensional? If so, how does the low dimensionality enable predictions with limited information? Here, we report an emergent simplicity that the temporal dynamics of observable microbial populations can be captured by low-dimensional representations. Using variational autoencoders, we define a critical latent dimension ( E c ) that operationally quantifies the smallest latent dimension required for high-fidelity reconstruction of observable microbial dynamics under a specified criterion. Despite the complexity of unobserved background dynamics, we find E c to be drastically lower than the community’s apparent degrees of freedom. E c scales linearly with the number of observables, providing an empirical principle for determining representation complexity. This principle holds across simulations of pairwise interacting communities, consumer–resource dynamics, spatially distributed microbial patches, and plasmid transfer, experiments with engineered and environment-derived communities, and human microbiomes. Our findings establish a scaling law for microbial community dynamics and demonstrate that low-dimensional representations of observable dynamics retain information useful for selected prediction tasks without direct measurement of the complete community.

fundamentals.title: Foiling Black Hole Foils: Revealing Horizon Alternatives with Baryonic Atmospheres
fundamentals.abstract: Event horizons are a defining feature of black holes. Consequently, there have been many efforts to probe their existence in astrophysical black hole candidates, spanning 10 orders of magnitude in mass. Nevertheless, horizons remain an obstacle to unifying general relativity and quantum mechanics, most sharply presented by the information paradox. This has motivated a proliferation of horizonless alternatives (black hole foils) that avoid event horizons and are therefore presumably benign. We explore the fate of accreting material in the context of spherically symmetric horizonless compact objects in the steady state regime. We find that for typical accreting astronomical targets, foils can develop an optically thick, convectively stable baryonic atmosphere, immediately implying the creation of an emitting photosphere at modest redshift even when the surface redshift is extreme. The emergent photosphere luminosity is driven toward the accretion powered equilibrium value and is only weakly sensitive to the foil redshift. Moreover, local gas–surface interaction provides a microphysical lower bound on the effective base temperature, insulating the atmosphere from arbitrarily cold foils. The unknown properties of the foil enter only through local boundary conditions controlling baryon processing and thermal coupling at the surface, making the solutions broadly applicable to horizonless alternatives that do not invoke significant additional nonlocal interactions. Thus, under minimal assumptions (GR exterior and local surface interactions), spherically symmetric horizonless foils in accreting systems are generically observationally exposed: the absence of a thermal photosphere directly constrains or rules out broad classes of such models.

fundamentals.title: Diffusion Models for Small-Molecule Design
fundamentals.abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have emerged as a class of generative models for controllable small-molecule design in drug discovery capable of progressively transforming noisy or partially specified molecular states into candidate structures under structural, geometric, and property constraints. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of the methodological foundations and representative applications of diffusion-based molecular generation, emphasizing the alignment among molecular representations, generative dynamics, controllable design, and evaluation and validation. Particular attention is given to recent advances in property- and structure-guided generation, target-aware and fragment-based design, multiobjective optimization, and synthesis-aware generation. We also discuss the roles of data sets, computational evaluation, and prospective experiments in assessing the chemical and biological relevance of generated molecules. By organizing these developments within a unified conceptual framework, we provide computational chemists and drug discovery researchers with a structured roadmap that balances the mathematical rigor with chemical intuition. Throughout, we highlight current methodological limitations and unresolved challenges and conclude with future directions toward chemically credible and experimentally grounded molecular design. To facilitate navigation of this rapidly evolving field, we introduce an interactive companion platform (https://diffsmd.scbdd.com) that provides a curated, continuously updated repository of model architectures and visualizations.

fundamentals.title: Bright Galaxies at Cosmic Dawn: A Cloud-Scale Star Formation Model Unifying Variable SFE, IMFs, and Stochasticity
fundamentals.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
fundamentals.abstract: To investigate the origins of the high abundance of UV-bright galaxies at z > 10, we present a new semi-analytic model that bridges the gap between small-scale star formation physics and large-scale galaxy evolution by explicitly tracking discrete star-forming clouds within smoothly evolving dark matter potentials. Unlike conventional semi-analytic models, our approach naturally captures the stochasticity of star formation, allowing us to isolate how cloud properties, star formation efficiencies (SFEs), and stellar initial mass functions (IMFs) shape the star-formation burstiness of early galaxies. Clouds are drawn sequentially from a cloud mass distribution, assigned an SFE and IMF depending on cloud mass, metallicity, and redshift, and evolve under the influence of short-timescale stellar feedback. We identify three distinct star formation regimes arising from the interplay between cloud masses, densities, and feedback timescales: a stochastic, feedback-limited regime in low-mass halos with long quiescent phases; a bursty regime regulated by the cloud mass distribution; and a smooth, continuous regime in massive halos. Our fiducial model adopts a dynamic IMF, an SFE linked to cloud properties and the IMF, and massive, moderately dense clouds. Varying assumptions reveals that top-heavy IMFs and enhanced SFEs in massive clouds amplify burstiness, while altering the upper cloud mass or density normalisation is secondary. Among model ingredients, the IMF most strongly impacts the UV luminosity function (LF), while switching to a constant SFE boosts the faint end, and reducing the maximum cloud mass decreases the bright end. These results demonstrate that cloud-scale physics critically shape early galaxy UV luminosity distributions.

fundamentals.title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals molecular organization of human and nonhuman primate basal ganglia
fundamentals.abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) are interconnected subcortical nuclei with a complex topographical organization that orchestrate goal-directed behaviors and are implicated in neurodegenerative movement disorders. We generated a cellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics atlas of the BG in human, rhesus macaque, and common marmoset, sampling over one million cells in each species. By integrating spatial data with a cross-species consensus single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) cell-type taxonomy, this atlas reveals principles of molecular organization within and across structures. Extensive spatial sampling across the rostral-caudal axis illuminates complex, yet highly stereotyped, multi-axis gene expression gradients superimposed onto discrete compartments of the striatum. Additionally, we identify core-shell organization of the internal globus pallidus. This unified, cross-species spatial transcriptomics atlas will be a foundational resource for characterizing the molecular and functional organization of the BG and their roles in health and disease.

fundamentals.title: The commutativity problem for effective varieties of formal series, and applications
fundamentals.abstract: A formal series in noncommuting variables Σ over the rationals is a mapping \(\Sigma ^* \rightarrow {\mathbb {Q}} \) from the free monoid generated by Σ to the rationals. We say that it is commutative if the output does not depend on the order of the symbols in the input. The commutativity problem for a class of series takes as input a (finite presentation of) a series from the class and amounts to establishing whether it is commutative. This is a very natural, albeit nontrivial problem, which has not been considered before from an algorithmic perspective. We show that commutativity is decidable for all classes of series that constitute a so-called effective prevariety , a notion generalising Reutenauer’s varieties of formal series. For example, the class of rational series , introduced by Schützenberger in the 1960’s, is well-known to be an effective (pre)variety, and thus commutativity is decidable for it. In order to showcase the applicability of our result, we consider classes of formal series generalising the rational ones. We consider polynomial automata , shuffle automata , and infiltration automata , and we show that each of these models recognises an effective prevariety of formal series. Consequently, their commutativity problem is decidable, which is a novel result. We find it remarkable that commutativity can be decided in a uniform way for such disparate computation models. Finally, we present applications of commutativity outside the theory of formal series. We show that we can decide solvability in sequences and in power series for restricted classes of algebraic difference and differential equations, for which such problems are undecidable in full generality. fundamentals.title: Electric Field Catalysis and the Metabolic Origin of Life
fundamentals.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
fundamentals.abstract: Metabolic theories for the origin of life postulate that chemical reaction networks emerged spontaneously from geochemistry and grew more complex due to positive feedback effects in catalysis. However, experimentally establishing protometabolic networks has proven challenging. In this Perspective, we make the case for electric field catalysis at charged aqueous interfaces as a crucial overlooked element for initiating protometabolic networks, an initial constraint that foreshadows the eventual takeover of electrostatic catalysis by enzymes. We first overview types of positive feedback relevant to the early evolution of metabolism, the theory of electric field catalysis, and its dominant role in enzyme catalysis. We then examine recent experiments and calculations highlighting the ability of external electric fields to enable nonenzymatic analogues of challenging metabolic reactions in micro- to millisecond reaction times. An underexplored mode of small molecule catalysis (reorientation catalysis) that can only operate in external electric fields is proposed to make positive feedback within prebiotic reaction networks more achievable. By embodying electrostatic catalysis, compartmentalization, and ion concentration gradients, charged aqueous interfaces prepattern three fundamental features of biology, making them a preferred environment for a metabolic origin of life. Making robust progress on the origin of life may surprisingly require exploring the nascent area of electric field-mediated chemistry at aqueous interfaces. Life does not use electric fields to catalyze its metabolic network by accident.

fundamentals.title: Substitutional Quantification and Arithmetical Truth
fundamentals.abstract: In the mid‐20th century, there was a debate about whether the quantifiers in first‐order logic should be understood objectually or substitutionally. This debate typically focused on ontology and assumed that we could use only one of these two types of quantification. After Kripke and others influentially argued that the two kinds of quantification were logically equivalent, defenses of substitutional quantification were rare. Following Gottlieb and Field, I argue that Kripke was wrong and that substitutional consequence is language‐bound and non‐compact. While of no help with ontology, I also argue that so‐understood, substitutional quantification can be applied to help explain our grasp of a determinate notion of arithmetical truth. To argue for this, I give an account of the metasemantics of the substitutional quantifiers and prove that adding a single, very natural, mixed axiom to weak theories of arithmetic results in a categorical theory. This approach promises to explain arithmetical truth on a less controversial basis than appeals to either second‐order logic or the omega rule, thus making progress on the project of explaining our grasp of arithmetic in a naturalistically acceptable fashion.

fundamentals.title: Tidal Deformation and Strain Accumulation of Solid Compact Stars
fundamentals.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
fundamentals.abstract: The tidal deformability of compact stars encodes the equation of state of dense matter, and gravitational-wave observations such as GW170817 have begun to constrain it under the assumption of a fluid interior. Yet whether the interior of pulsar-like compact stars is fluid or solid remains largely untested, despite the distinct tidal responses the two states predict. In this work, based on the strangeon-star model, we develop a framework for modeling tidal deformation in solid compact stars. Adopting a shear modulus of μ = 1034 erg cm−3, we find a relative difference of approximately 30 % in tidal deformability between solid and fluid strangeon stars of 1.4 M⊙, corresponding to a ~10 % deviation from the universal I–Love relation. We further model the accumulation of internal strain during binary inspiral and find that it peaks near the stellar center. When the gravitational-wave frequency reaches several hundred $\rm Hz$, the strain in a large fraction of the stellar volume exceeds the adopted threshold σ = 10−3, and the elastic energy stored in the threshold-exceeding region reaches ~1046 erg at these frequencies. A solid-to-fluid transition would alter the tidal response and could imprint on the waveform and phase of the emitted gravitational radiation. Combined with the precursor electromagnetic emission, these gravitational-wave signatures offer a multi-messenger avenue to test the solid nature of pulsar-like compact stars.

fundamentals.title: Solving the Dual Puzzles of Collective Harm
fundamentals.abstract: Suppose some uncoordinated group of agents causes tremendous harm, but none of the individuals could have meaningfully changed this result by acting differently. These “collective harm” cases have been the subject of extended philosophical discussion, but this paper argues that there are really two different, if connected, puzzles presented by such cases: (1) a puzzle about how to characterize the moral injury to those who suffer this harm (the “wrongness puzzle”) and (2) a puzzle about why agents may do something wrong in participating in producing this harm (the “participation puzzle”). This paper elaborates these puzzles, defends the idea that they are different from each other, and offers solutions to them both. The core idea is that an application of the distinction between ideal and nonideal theory can shed light on both puzzles; the injury experienced by the victims of collective harm is to be understood in terms of the shortfall they suffer from how they would fare if ideal circumstances obtained, and participation in collective harm is wrong when it involves reasoning that fails to appropriately apply ideal moral rules to nonideal situations.

fundamentals.title: A Log-Uniform Initial Magnetic Field Distribution Explains Pulsar and Magnetar Populations through Magnetic Inclination Alignment
fundamentals.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
fundamentals.abstract: The origin of the gap in the observed magnetic field distribution between pulsars and magnetars raises a challenge to understanding these populations within a unified framework. We analytically show that the gap can be naturally explained by the alignment of the magnetic inclination angle between the magnetic and spin axes. Based on coupled evolution of spin-down and magnetic inclination angle in the plasma-filled magnetosphere, the alignment timescale follows τα∝B−2. Thus, strongly magnetized neutron stars including high-B pulsars and magnetars align more rapidly than pulsars with 1012 G, reducing their beaming fraction and thereby suppressing their observed numbers. However, magnetars are primarily identified through X-ray activity and are therefore relatively less affected by beaming. Taking into account both beaming fraction and luminosity corrections, we reconstruct the initial magnetic field distribution from the observed distribution. We show that pulsars and magnetars do not dictate intrinsically distinct initial distributions, but can instead be understood within a single continuous initial magnetic field distribution, such as a log-uniform distribution.

fundamentals.title: On the Orbital Evolution of Giant-planet Pair Embedded in a Gaseous Disk. III. Simultaneous Gas Accretion and the Final Mass Ratio
fundamentals.abstract: Recent exoplanet surveys reveal a systematic trend in the mass ratios of giant-planet pairs (>30 M ⊕ ). Although the M outer / M inner is broadly centered near unity, it exhibits a dependence on orbital separation. Compact pairs tend to have comparable masses, whereas widely separated pairs show outer-heavy configurations. To investigate the origin of this trend, we perform 2D hydrodynamic simulations that couple gas accretion and orbital migration of two giant planet embryos with initial masses of 15−30 M ⊕ . We explore the effects of disk viscosity, surface density slope, and initial mass ratio on the coupled evolution of planetary growth and migration. We find that convergent migration drives the planets to open a common gap, restructuring the gas flow. This configuration induces asymmetric accretion, in which the inner planet becomes starved as gap clearing suppresses its gas supply, while the outer planet continues to accrete from the high-density region at the outer gap edge. Consequently, the system naturally evolves toward mass-ratio convergence, and in many cases produces an inversion of the initial core-mass hierarchy. We further show that migration outcomes are highly sensitive to initial conditions. Systems with initially more massive inner cores tend to diverge, whereas steeper surface density profiles and more massive outer cores favor convergent migration and subsequent resonance capture. Overall, our results identify common-gap-driven asymmetric accretion as a unified mechanism linking orbital architecture, resonant capture, and the observed mass-ratio demographics of giant planet pairs.

fundamentals.title: A Unified Reactivity Scale Predicts Nonenzymatic Phosphoryl Transfer and Nucleophilic Catalysis in Water
fundamentals.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
fundamentals.abstract: The transfer of phosphoryl groups plays a central role in biochemical energy metabolism. Understanding how such reactions could have occurred before the emergence of enzymes is thus crucial for elucidating the chemical foundations of life. Although the factors governing the mechanisms of phosphoryl transfer in water are well understood, predicting whether a given nucleophile and phosphorylating agent will undergo productive phosphoryl transfer rather than hydrolysis remains difficult, thereby hindering the rational exploration of nonenzymatic phosphorylation reactions. Herein, we establish a quantitative reactivity scale that predicts absolute rate constants for nonenzymatic phosphoryl transfer reactions in water based on a linear free-energy relationship (LFER). Using high-throughput kinetics, we measured 11,520 phosphoryl transfer reactions for 145 unique combinations of nucleophiles and phosphorylating agents under varying reaction conditions. Mechanism-specific rate constants extracted from this data for 102 substrate pairs, together with values scraped from the literature, enabled us to parametrize an LFER that places 34 phosphorylating agents and 45 nucleophiles on a unified quantitative reactivity scale, enabling predictions across 14 orders of magnitude in reactivity. Finally, we show that the empirically derived reactivity parameters can be used to predict optimal nucleophilic catalysts by balancing the competing steps in catalytic turnover, as experimentally validated for the reaction of monoamidophosphate with pyridines. For phosphorylating agents of intermediate electrophilicity such as ATP, imidazole is predicted to be the optimal catalyst, offering a kinetic rationale for the prevalence of histidine residues in enzymatic phosphoryl transfer.
